descripcion: Criteria NASA names for choosing a base or crewed landing site on the Moon (south pole) and Mars, and the sources of the layers that measure them (web/data/sitio). Each entry carries a literal quotation checked against its source by scripts/verificar_citas.py. A number is used only if the quotation gives it.

criterios.organismo: NASA (news release, Artemis III candidate regions)
criterios.cita: Each of these regions is located within six degrees of latitude of the lunar South Pole

criterios.organismo: NASA (news release, Artemis III candidate regions)
criterios.cita: Access to sunlight is critical for a long-term stay at the Moon because it provides a power source and minimizes temperature variations.
criterios.nota: NASA gives no minimum share of sunlight; the 6.5 days in the same release are the length of one mission, not a threshold for the layer

criterios.cita: You want to land in the flattest area possible, since you don't want the landing vehicle to tip over
criterios.nota: NASA publishes no maximum slope for the base or the lander

criterios.cita: it must offer easy access to areas of complete darkness that hold water ice.

no_medidos.nombre: Line of sight to Earth for communications
no_medidos.organismo: NASA (LPSC abstract, Artemis III regions update)
no_medidos.cita: If Artemis III employs a Direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication architecture, regions with greater Earth visibility are preferred.

no_medidos.organismo: NASA (news release, Artemis III regions update)
no_medidos.cita: Factors in the selection process included science potential, launch window availability, terrain suitability, communication capabilities with Earth, and lighting conditions.

no_medidos.organismo: NASA (news release, Artemis III candidate regions)
no_medidos.cita: Specific landing sites are tightly coupled to the timing of the launch window, so multiple regions ensure flexibility to launch throughout the year.
no_medidos.motivo: depends on the mission date, not on the place alone

no_medidos.organismo: NASA (LPSC abstract, Artemis III regions update)
no_medidos.cita: including impact craters, block populations, and rough or highly variable terrain
no_medidos.motivo: no boulder or small-crater layer; the slope layer is a mean over 293 m cells

no_medidos.nombre: Landing area at least 1 km from the habitat
no_medidos.cita: The landing area, ideally, should be separated from other base camp features — such as the habitat or solar panels — by at least half a mile, or 1 kilometer.
no_medidos.motivo: a layout rule inside the base, not a property of one point

criterios.organismo: NASA (Bussey and Hoffman, human landing sites workshop slides)
criterios.cita: Preliminary latitude boundaries set at +/- 50 degrees

criterios.organismo: NASA (Bussey and Hoffman, IEEE Aerospace Conference)
criterios.cita: (b) less than +2 kilometers altitude (Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) reference)

criterios.organismo: NASA (Bussey and Hoffman, IEEE Aerospace Conference)
criterios.cita: an area of approximately 25 square kilometers within which the terrain is generally level (slopes less than ~10 degrees)

criterios.organismo: NASA (Bussey and Hoffman, IEEE Aerospace Conference, Appendix B)
criterios.cita: The raw material can be in the form of ice, ice/regolith mix, or hydrated minerals, and the top of the raw material deposit should be as close to the surface as possible.
criterios.nota: the numbers NASA gives for this resource (> 100 t of water, < 3 km from the plant) cannot be read from a neutron map

no_medidos.nombre: Thick fine dust (very low thermal inertia, high albedo)
no_medidos.organismo: NASA (Bussey and Hoffman, IEEE Aerospace Conference)
no_medidos.cita: does not contain thick deposits of fine-grained dust (e.g., extremely low thermal inertia and high albedo).
no_medidos.motivo: no layer in this version; NASA gives no number

no_medidos.nombre: Landing hazards: craters, dunes, chaotic terrain
no_medidos.organismo: NASA (Bussey and Hoffman, IEEE Aerospace Conference)
no_medidos.cita: significantly devoid of landing hazards (e.g., large and/or closely concentrated craters, mountainous terrain, broken/jumbled/chaotic terrain, extensive dune fields, etc.)
no_medidos.motivo: no hazard layer; the slope layer is at 3.7 km pixels

no_medidos.nombre: Water resource less than 3 km from the processing plant
no_medidos.organismo: NASA (Bussey and Hoffman, IEEE Aerospace Conference, Appendix B)
no_medidos.cita: The raw material must be located less than 3 kilometers from the ISRU processing plant and power infrastructure
no_medidos.motivo: the neutron map shows hydrogen in 0.5° cells, not tonnes of water nor distances of 3 km

no_medidos.organismo: NASA (Bussey and Hoffman, IEEE Aerospace Conference, Appendix A)
no_medidos.cita: Noachian and/or Hesperian rocks in stratigraphic context that have high likelihood of containing trapped atmospheric gasses.

fuentes_dato.organismo: NASA PDS Geosciences Node (MGS MOLA MEGDR label)
fuentes_dato.cita: Each sample represents median observed topography within a 0.0625 by 0.0625 degree area.

fuentes_dato.organismo: NASA PDS Geosciences Node (MGS MOLA MEGDR label)
fuentes_dato.cita: Topography is the planetary radius minus the areoid radius at a given longitude and latitude.

fuentes_dato.nombre: Mars Odyssey Neutron Spectrometer, epithermal neutron flux
fuentes_dato.organismo: NASA PDS Geosciences Node (Mars Odyssey GRS special product label)
fuentes_dato.cita: The figures are maps of thermal, epithermal, and fast neutron flux measured by the Neutron Spectrometer over the first 25.7 days of mapping.

fuentes_dato.nombre: Mars Odyssey Neutron Spectrometer, epithermal neutron flux
fuentes_dato.organismo: NASA PDS Geosciences Node (Mars Odyssey GRS special product label)
fuentes_dato.cita: Epithermal neutron flux for the given 0.5 by 0.5 degree area, in counts per second.
Soil enriched by hydrogen is indicated by the deep blue colors on the map, which show a low intensity of epithermal neutrons.

fuentes_dato.nombre: Seasonal CO2 frost hides hydrogen in the far north
fuentes_dato.cita: Hydrogen in the far north is hidden at this time beneath a layer of carbon dioxide frost (dry ice).
